critiques.summary:
Every round-1 gap that was blocking has been closed with direct, independent measurements, and H1 is now the only hypothesis consistent with the full picture.

Closed since round 1: (a) the portfolio-service side is no longer inferred — F24 shows its p99 rising ~26x (185ms -> 4701ms) at exactly 08:57Z with request_rate and error_rate flat (F25), i.e. it degraded first, at/just before the DB step, and in a latency-only pattern consistent with executing a slow read; (b) ledger-db resource state is measured, not inferred — F30 cpu_pct steps 30.53 -> 95.99 in one step and holds 95-97%, while F31 disk_used_pct and F34 replication_lag_ms are perfectly flat, so "shared-DB saturation" is CPU-bound and actually observed; (c) the onset-minute conflict I flagged in round 1 is resolved — F32/F33 pin the step to the single 08:58:00Z minute (slow queries 1.33 -> 139.17, connections 60.10 -> 185.11), showing F9/F10/F12's 08:51 bucket was coarse-bucket artifact, not an earlier onset; (d) the scope objection is answered — F26/F27/F28 show the two other co-tenants flat within ~2%, so the blast radius is exactly the changed workload's service plus order-service, which is what a specific unindexed query predicts and what uniform DB saturation does not; (e) F19/F20 close the deployment enumeration across all services for 05-03 through 05-05 with zero for order-service.

Temporal ordering is now tight and discriminating: cfg-2903 at 08:00Z produced no CPU or slow-query step across the following 58 minutes (F22, F30), while dep-5905 at 08:56Z precedes the 08:58Z step by 2 minutes and its change description ("new query on trades filtered by account_id + executed_at", "no migration included") matches F11's logged Seq Scan statement text. H2's mechanism (scale_factor acting on a bloat timescale) also cannot produce a one-minute cliff, so H2 is contradicted on mechanism as well as timing. H3 is contradicted by flat disk_used_pct and replication_lag_ms against a 96% CPU step; H4 by zero order-service changes plus the DB-side statement attribution and DB-first ordering. HIST-111 is a matched precedent (new unindexed report query -> seq scans on ledger-db, fixed by adding an index).

Remaining uncertainty is secondary and does not change the fix: the missing-index premise rests on the observed Seq Scan over 48.2M rows (F11) rather than on a pg_indexes read, which the toolset cannot perform, and per-query volume attribution to the new endpoint is not isolated. Both would matter only if the fix were ambiguous — it is not: add the index / roll back dep-5905 either way. That is why this is a lower confidence cap rather than another evidence round.

challenges.issue: The missing-index premise is supported only by the observed Seq Scan plan (F11) over 48.2M rows; no index inventory (pg_indexes) or EXPLAIN was obtainable, and F21 only establishes that no DDL appears in deployment/config records. The plan text itself is strong direct evidence of a seq scan, so this is corroboration shortfall rather than a plausible competing origin.

That the new dep-5905 endpoint actually drove the query flood is inferred from application_name=portfolio-service on the logged statement plus the verbatim match of the query text to dep-5905's change description (F2/F11/F13); per-endpoint query volume was not isolated. The textual match and the 08:56->08:57/08:58 timing make alternative sources of the same statement shape implausible.

Asymmetric co-tenant impact (portfolio-service + order-service degraded; payment-service and settlement-service flat, F26-F28) requires an explanation consistent with 'shared DB saturation'. Order-service's pool rose 14 -> 46 (F12) and it holds long write transactions, which plausibly explains why it times out while lower-volume readers do not; the asymmetry slightly narrows the mechanism from uniform saturation to contention on write paths, but does not redirect the root cause.

cfg-2903 is excluded on timing and mechanism, not on direct autovacuum runtime telemetry (no autoanalyze/vacuum/bloat metrics are exposed). Given the 58-minute effect-free interval, the one-minute onset cliff, and the attributable statement signature, this does not merit further querying.

IOPS throttling / burst-credit exhaustion (the HIST-110 precedent, F6) cannot be measured directly because ledger-db exposes no IOPS/iowait metric; exclusion rests on flat disk_used_pct and replication_lag_ms plus a CPU-bound 96% plateau with an attributable query. Acceptable as a contradiction, though not a direct meter reading.

Order-service CPU/memory/GC and request_rate/error_rate were never retrieved, so 'order-service is a wait victim, not a source' rests on zero deployments (F20), no config change, DB-first ordering, and pool-fill-as-wait evidence (F12). A spontaneous order-service-side saturation would not produce the portfolio-service-attributed seq-scan flood, so this is not a live competing origin.
